blocks.x: This tape is being recorded in the back room of the Mardi Gras Lounge, 333 Bourbon Street. The date is January 18, 1951. Present at this time are R.W. Greenwood and Richard B. Allen.
Talk on, you know what you want to tell me?
Okay. I think, Lizzie, the first thing we're interested in finding out is when were you born?
I was born on March the 31st, 1895.
1895 in New Orleans?
Right here in New Orleans on Bourbon Street.
Were your father and mother musical people?

My mother sings, but not publicly. Only until after she got in her old days, she started singing in old folks' concerts and singing old Creole songs, but when she was young, she didn't. She didn't? Mm-hmm.
Did they send you for musical instruction when you were young?
No, no. My mother wasn't able to send me to how I started singing in my catechism school.
Oh.

Mrs. Atkin had a little private catechism school, and most all the neighborhood children attended the school. She used to teach us how to sing and dance. She'd give little concerts on Sundays for the neighborhood, you know, charge 10, 15 cents out in her backyard. They'd build a little, take some wood and build a little platform and get benches and put out there. And most of the whole neighborhood would turn out to see us kids singing, dancing, and go on. And finally, it just got to be such a big thing that everybody started doing it. Pretty in every ward, every now and then, you'd hear of a concert, usually on Sundays and on holidays. And, of course, all the children who were the best were the ones that they would get to come and perform. And then they'd pay us, give us 50 cents, 75 cents. Well, it went up to $1.50, $2.00. Well, we just started, as we started getting bigger and bigger, we started getting bigger pay. Then I started getting offers from the halls, then France Amie Hall, Lekite Hall, Artesian Hall, Hopes Hall, Gloves Hall, Tokyo. Finally, the Dixie Park, the Lincoln Park, then the Pithian Temple, then the Pithian Theater. Then finally, I, well, they just thought I was so good, and they asked me to go away on the shows. And I did. My sister's show. My sister Edna, Benbo, and her husband had a show. So then I left with them, and we was playing all around here in Louisiana. Bugaloosa, Slidell, and my sister was what they used to call a long time ago a coon-shouter. About when was that? Well, I was the, as I started up, I started out, when I made my first communion. I was singing, I was then singing little concerts before I made my first communion. It was during my catechism class that I started, you know, small child.
When you sang at the halls, did they have a band?

Oh, sure. Or usually it would be what they call a concert and ball, meaning the concert would start at about 8, 8.30 and last until about 10, 30, 11 o'clock. Well, when it was given in halls like that in order to make money so they could charge, you know, 50 cents and 75 cents, they had to have a band. That's where I started working with Kid Oliver and Ori and all of those different musicians, you know, P. Kool and Manuel Perez and all, you know, Bunk Johnson. That's all of that. It's in those times that I sang with those fellas. They'd hire them, you know, they'd play for the concert. Then after, they'd play for them to dance. And the dance would last maybe until 3, 4 o'clock in the morning.
Now, what about your name? We want to get that down straight. How did you happen to get the name Lizzie Miles?

Well, they said, just like for a good billing, they'd say, Miles, I used to be smiling all the time. They said, Miles of smiles from Lizzie Miles. But my name is Elizabeth. Elizabeth Mary Landreau. That's my maiden name. And then my marriage name is Elizabeth Pajot.
Pajot, is that the same as Willie Pajot?
That's right. That's right. Willie Pajot and my husband's first cousin.
Oh, I see.

That's right. So then they called me Lizzie Miles. Well, it was an easy name to say. Pajot would have been too hard to say. They'd have been calling me Pago and Pajo, which they do right now. That's how they pronounce the name. Very few people pronounce it Pajo. They call me Pajo, Ponge, Pango, and everything but Pajo.
Well, the Miles name, was it just made up or was there, in other words, just because you were smiling, they made up the Miles?
Well, that's how the idea started, you know, see. Miles of smiles from Lizzie Miles.
Who were some of the singers that you admired when you were young?

Well, the first singer that I would go every week to see when she was here was Sophie Tucker. She played at the Palace Theater here, and they used to charge 10 cents to go into Pitt. And on Saturdays, I'd hurry up and get my work through, so my mother would let me go up there to listen to her singing. The first song I ever heard her sing was that mesmerizing, meddlesome tune. I've never forgotten it.
Well, what about blues singers? Did you like any blues singers in those days? How did you feel about blues?

Well, I admired my sister, because my sister was, they used to call them, like I told you, coon shouters, you know. And she could shout, and then she used to roll her eyes for one solid chorus. She wouldn't do nothing but just roll, do a whole chorus rolling her eyes, and I went home and went in front of the mirror to see if I could do it. But I never could do it. I never did learn to roll my eyes like my sister, but she could shout, you know. She was a real, what they call a coon shouter.
Any other sisters that signed?
No, no, no, just her.
What about uncles, cousins, brothers, anybody else?
Not that I know of. Not that I know of. Because there's a lot of my family on my father's side that I don't know. No, I don't know, so I don't know whether they, you know, was any singers among them.
Any of them musicals?
That I don't know, because I don't know them. So many of them I don't know.
Of these, did you hear any of the big famous blues singers when you're down here, people like Ma Rainey or Bessie Smith?

Oh, yeah, I worked with Ma Rainey, like we played what you call day and date, you know. I was sure maybe, I was sure in one theater, her show in another theater like that, you know, see. Sure, I heard Ma Rainey, in fact, I heard them all, Bessie Smith, Clara Smith, Mamie Smith, you know. Who of them did you like the best? Well, when I first heard the first record of Mamie Smith, the Crazy Blues, I liked it fine, you know. Yeah, and I liked her style, I liked her way of singing. That was the first blues record in the late, yeah, late. But they had been, they claimed that they had been, I did know her, I knew her, but I'd forgotten her name. Now, I think, no, it wasn't, it wasn't, it wasn't O'Vara Johnson, who had went to Europe with this white performer that taken, she was the first one that went to Europe and taken colored performers with her. Well, they claimed they had made a record a long time ago on the Victor, you know, singing blues, but it was never, I don't think, you know, made popular like Mamie Smith. I think Mamie Smith is the first real popular blues singer, Mamie Smith. She sang that Crazy Blues.
Well, who were some of the singers around town that were prominent on the order of Ma Rainey? You mean here in New Orleans? In New Orleans, did you hear her?

Her name was, oh, she was Dad James' wife. Dad James was a sort of a producer and a comedian that gave shows around. Tilly Johnson, Tilly Johnson. She was, I think, one of the, you know, another, what I call, coon shouter, too, you know.
Ann Cook singing when you were coming out?
Oh, well, no, Ann Cook, that's before my time. That was before my time. Though I've met Ann Cook and she's told me about her, you know, her singing, but I never heard her sing.
Where was your very first job working as a featured entertainer with a band?

Well, it's like I'm telling you, in the concerts, you see, when I was small, it was not, they never said about featured, they just had the show and all of us kids went on. But the first cabaret job, the first time I ever worked in a nightclub was right here in New Orleans out in Bucktown for Martins. And a friend of mine was playing out there in a band and he just asked me to take a ride out there and I did. And when he introduced me to the band boys, he told them how I could sing. So Manuel Mineta was the leader of this orchestra. Oh, I know that band. Well, and he said to me, well, come on, we can play anything you can sing. So I said, okay, then, let's go on Dardanella. And they played Dardanella and I sang Dardanella and I got the job that night.
Who was in the band? Who else?

Well, now I see, there was Manuel Mineta and there was, um, I can't, I can't, I think, I think Carrie Fritz was the, I think Carrie was the cornet player. And, um, they had a cornet, I think banjo or guitar, I'm not sure, I can't remember so well. But, um, I think there was a piano, either banjo or a guitar, cornet, Amos White was playing the cornet. He's now in Oakland, California, Amos White, cornet player. He was cornet and they had drums and trombone and manual on the piano.
Did they have a clarinet?
Yes, I think, yes, and the clarinet player, oh, I can't remember his name.
Zip, was it Zip?
I think so, I think that's right, Zip. That's right, that's true, that's right, Zip.
I've heard prof speak about it, I used to think from prof.
Yeah, Zip, that's right, Zip.
He had a good old band, uh, they used to have Rene with him at one time.
Well, no, Rene wasn't with him at that time. I think it was, uh, Carrie, Carrie Fritz, I think, was with him at that time.

Yeah, but I mean, uh, I didn't buck down, he used to have Rene with him, he said. That's right, that's right. With Zip. But this band didn't have any trombone, I remember. Yeah. Mineta was playing piano with it?
That's right, Mineta was playing the piano.
He's a wonderful musician, he can play anything.

That's the first time I met Manuel then, out there. And so then I stayed there and I worked a while and I got the idea then that I liked it. Because I didn't like Cabaret Week. Before when I was working in the theaters and on the carnival shows and things, every city that I would be near or I played into, I would go, like at night, going out stepping, and I'd go to a cabaret. Well, as soon as they knew that I was singing, they'd ask me to do a number, they'd offer me a job. But, ooh, I didn't like that. I didn't like that close contact with the people. You could hear everything they said, all the remarks they would make, and I said, no, I wouldn't work. And when I was in Chicago, Tony Jackson, a great piano player from here, he was playing at the Teen Ann Jones'. I think they called it the Eli Number One. And so he introduced me to Teen Ann Jones. I've got the rose still that he gave me after I got through singing. I've got the petals in a Bible, you know. He gave it to me and I put it in a Bible and I still got it. After I got through singing and they offered me a job, but I didn't like it. I didn't want no cabaret work. I didn't like it. But then after I worked in Bucktown and they treated me so nice and I made so much money, they used to just throw five dollars out there. Well, that was the time, you know, the Storyville was going full blast then. So all of the people from there used to come out after hours, you know. And I made plenty of money out there. So that made me like it. Well, then I went to Chicago. And I arrived in Chicago on, I think it was a Tuesday night. And that Wednesday night we went out cabaret and our first place was, I wanted to go where King Oliver was playing. And that was the dreamland. And we went there. And as soon as King saw me, well, right away he requested a song. And I said, oh, I don't know what to sing. He said, well, come on. Ain't nobody around here singing Sister Kate. Come on and sing Sister Kate. And so I got out there and I said, and there was a little midget selling cigars and cigarettes. And I said, I'm not going to do no shimmying, though I'll sing the song. But I ain't going to shimmy like Sister Kate. And he says, well, I'll shimmy for you. And there I was out there singing the little midget was doing the shimmying. And so then I got a job that night. They hired me that night. And I stayed there and I worked with King. Well, he had Louis Armstrong was playing carnet. And Lil was playing. That was before he married Lil. Lil Harding, her name was then. She was at the piano. I think Dodds, I think Baby Dodds was playing drums. I think Eddie Garland was on the bass. Eddie Garland was on bass. Well, anyway, that's a bunch. Well, I stayed there and work. And then when I left there, I went Freddie Keper after me to come work at the entertainers. That was on 35th Street, Izzy Shaw's place, black and tan. And I went there. But I had a kind of a hard gang to buck up against there. They were mostly all dancers, you see, no singers. And so naturally, he wanted somebody who could sing, you see. And usually the singer, you know, always gets requested. So you'd make quite a bit of money. And they would just keep doing all sorts of things to, you know, make confusion. So finally, I just got disgusted. And I told him I was quitting. And oh, he didn't want me to quit, you know. And Freddie tried to talk to me, but I wouldn't stay. So I had an offer to go to work at the Deluxe for prayer. So right away, I just left and went to work at the Deluxe for prayer. And with Glover Compton. He's a great piano player, too.
He's still in Chicago.
With Glover Compton?
Yeah.
Yeah, that's right.
He knew why I know him.

Yeah? And his wife was an entertainer, too. She was then Nettie Lewis. She was a singer and dancer. Well, and I worked there with him and his wife. Then I came back home. I left and I came back to New Orleans. How when was this? Was it after the war? After the war? After the first war. Oh, yes, because the first war was around 1970 to 18, huh?
Yes.

Oh, well, 19, that time then. Yeah, that was before. That was after that. That was after that. Yeah. Because before that, I was with a circus during the time of the war. I was with a 35-car circus. Jones Brothers and Wilson Circus. Three-wing circus. I used to sing in a side show with the band. And I used to sing in the big show, in the concert with the band over there. And I used to ride in the street parade with the elephant. And that was during the flu epidemic when they closed all the shows in the theaters. Well, then that's where I caught the flu. I had the flu. And the doctor told me I should stop singing for at least a year. And I had signed up to go with the LG Barnes Circus in Venice, California. Well, after the doctor. Well, during my sickness, you know. He said that after I got so that he could tell me. He told me that twice they had walked out the room, thought I was dying. They said I had got double pneumonia. And he said that one of my lungs was affected. So I mustn't sing. I must not sing for at least a year. Well, I stopped singing for, I think, about a year and a half. Almost two years before I did any singing. And that's right after that is when I went to Bucktown. That's why Amos came by. He used to come and get me to take me to get fresh air. You know, tell me to go and get fresh air. And that's how he just asked me to come right out there to Bucktown. I was going out there to get fresh air.
Well, when you came back to New Orleans from Chicago, what happened then? Did you work any music jobs or anything?

You mean here in the city? Yes. No, no. I didn't. I didn't. I just came and visited with my mother, you know. And then I went back. I went back to Chicago. And when I went back to Chicago, there was a producer around there, Jerry Mills, a stage producer, putting on shows. And he had a job for me in Springfield, Illinois, in a cabaret there. And I went. There was a great. He's a great pianist now, but I can't think of his name that I met there. And he was a young fellow just starting then, you know, playing in this place. And I stayed there a while then when my time was up and I returned to Chicago. That's when I met Spencer Williams, the writer of the Bass and Street Blues. And I was at the Royal Garden with King Oliver. And he asked me how I'd like to go to New York to make records. And I told him I'd like it fine.

if I was gonna make any money, you know. And so he told me, well, the idea was he had the telegram. He showed me the telegram from the Victor in the Columbia, telling him to bring a blues singer for audition, you know. And so he said, I would get all my transportation paid and everything, and I told him, could I get an advance? I wanted to make sure. So he said, yes, he asked me what I wanted, I told him. And so then I said, well, I'd go, and I went to New York and made a test for the Columbia and the OK, and Jimmy McHugh of the Mills staff, music staff, taking me to the Victor and played my first test on the Victor, dear old Southland. He wanted them to hear me, hear my voice, you know. And he figured that that would be the song to sing so they could see the volume of my voice and so on. Then Russell Robertson, piano player, I think he's out of Memphis. And he was working hard to get me the job as blues singer with the Blackbirds. But it was one of those things where, you know, it's like we say politics. And this Perry Bradford who had discovered Mamie Smith, he was then working on Edith Wilson. And so he got Edith Wilson in there, you see. Russell, he told me all how it was done and everything, you know. So then that's how Edith Wilson got the job in with Blackbirds. And then I start working around the nightclubs in New York. My first nightclub in New York was out at a place called Dash's Inn. It was opening up for Easter. And I got in town just about the time for the grand opening. And so they wanted a new face, you know. They didn't want anybody around town. And so I happened to be stopping with Lucille Hegeman, a blues singer you might know of her. Her husband was a piano player, Hegeman. He had a band. I think he, but when he took his band to Japan, I don't think he ever came back. I think he stayed over there. And last we heard, he had married a Japanese girl over there, and had raised a family and stayed over there and never came back. Well, they are the ones who recommended me to this Dash's Inn. And that's when I started working. While I was working there, I got an offer then to come to a, there was a man gonna see how a big cabaret would go in New York, you know, in Harlem. They had all those small places, you know, little small. And he opened a place that was a block long, the capital on Lenox Avenue between 139 and 40, I think it was. So naturally, he was out scouting around to get all the new talent he could. And his manager, assistant manager came where I was working, started talking to me about coming to work there. Then that was right in the heart of Harlem. So then they offered me a nice salary, and I left where I was at and went there. Well, I worked there, I guess, about three years. And that's where I left. Then Billy Pierce then was starting to book people for Paris, for the Moulin Rouge. And he had a bunch of girls he had booked up to go. And he said, you want to see if I want to go. And well, I told him, no, I wasn't interested in no theater work. And so then there was an entertainer who I had worked with, who went to Paris, Bricktop. And she was writing letters back of all the money she was making, you know. And so, well, I knew if Bricktop was making that kind of money, well, I had to say brag it on myself. I knew I was a better singer than her. So I figured I want to go there and get some of that money too. So then I was talking to the band and the piano player, Danny Wilson, maybe you know of him. He wrote that piece, With Someone Like You Around Me, How Could I Feel Blue? Beautiful number it is. Well, he said, I think I'll go over there. Then there was a saxophone and violin player, Ali Laguerre. He said, well, maybe I'll make the trip. I said, well, why not the three of us get together and we go together and we stick together and we look for work over there. It'll be us three. So that's how we planned it. And we said, okay. So we put our hands together and we did. And we left on the France, on the French liner, France or Paris, I think, one of the French boats anyway. We left and we went to Paris. And we happened to get in there just when a place was going to open up. Mrs. Regina Buchen, she was opening up a nightclub. And there was an American from America named Louis Mitchell. He was going to be in charge of the place, you see. And most all of those French places over there at that time, they would have American, they had American, you know, musicians and entertainers. And they would have the place named after them because they'd done the interpreting with the customers, you see. So they named the place Chez Michels, you see. But he was just the manager, you know, same way as they had a place named Chez Florence. Well, Florence Jones and her husband Palmer Jones were the entertainers there, you see. But it was a French woman who owned the place. And Bricktop, then she was working at, on Rue Pigalle. And they call it Chez Bricktop, you see. But she was working for a Frenchman, too. So then I went in there with myself, Danny Wilson, and Lily Gare. We went in there at this place, Chez Michels, you see. But it seems as though he had, he was with the place where Florence was. And this woman thought that he was going to, you know, take all the business away from there and come there, but it seems as though he didn't draw as well as she thought he was going to. So then she let him go and took in a troop of Russians. Alexander Storzynski and a troop of Russians. And in this troop, there was two, do the Russians have princes and prince? Well, there was two princes and two prince that was singing in the chorus. And they used to just talk my head off back there about America. And, oh, how they would love to come to America. And then they compared our salary with the salary they was getting over there. You see, we were getting double to what they got, you know. And so that's where I got the name of the Black Rose and La Rose Noire. And they had black satin roses that would give to each customer, you see. And when they'd introduce me, they would introduce me as La Rose Noire, you know, the Black Rose. And I was then doing a couple of Sidney Bechet's number, Do That Thing. And in this song, it said something about poke chops. So those people, all they could say was poke chops when they wanted the song. They said, sing poke chop, poke chop. Oh, so... Well, okay, let's see what we're going to do.

I wanted to ask you a few questions about your phonograph record. I know this is going to be kind of hard on your memory. But do you remember who you made Grieving Mama Blues and Slow Up Papa with? Oh, that's on the OK. With Piana and Cornette.

On the OK? With Piana and Cornette? Yeah. Well... No, I can't remember because... Well, I mean, you see, by not having my own accompaniment, I had to just sing with anybody that they would just get, you know? And they just would... Every time I went there, there was somebody different, you know? But I don't remember who that cornette player or piano player was. But did you look on the record? They usually put the name on the record. No, it's not on that record. No. Slow Up Papa.
Slow Up Papa. What about those OKs?

Well, the OK records, you see, those were the first records that I made, and it was with a white band there that played by music. They didn't play by like that, no Dixieland, no jazz, nothing like that. They strictly played music. And most of their arrangements was made for them by Bob Rickards. So I don't remember the names of the musicians, either. You know?
Yeah. What about this fellow, Clarence Johnson?
Well, he was from Chicago. He was quite a piano player. Yes, he was quite a piano player. And I did quite a few records with him.
You know, I looked through here and I didn't find any list in here of Russell Robinson on Brunswick with you. You say you made a record with him?
That's right. I made the Haitian blues. Haitian blues, I think, and Black Man Be On Your Way. On the Brunswick.
They got that as Clarence Johnson and Spencer Williams.
I mean, the writers who wrote the piece. They wrote the piece.
Oh, they wrote the piece?

They're the writers of the piece. Clarence Williams is, I mean, Spencer Williams is the writer of the Haitian blues. See? But Russell Robinson is the one who played the piano. And you played the gazook. And I played the gazook. That's right.
Oh, I see.
Yeah.
What about Man of War blues and electrician blues?
Well, that was on the Victor.
Don't Throw It My Key Away is another one.
That's with Jelly Roll Morton.
That is with Jelly Roll Morton. Well, this is fine.
Jelly Roll Morton.
On Victor.

On Victor. But no, the Man of War was with Leroy Smith's piano player. What's his name? Let me see. If I can think of his name. Oh, I don't remember his name. He was a piano player playing with Leroy Smith's orchestra. Leroy Smith was playing then at the time at Shuffle Inn.
Well, we'll look it up later. I got it probably in a bucket home.
Yeah.
Now, you did make records with Jelly Roll, though. I know you told me about that.
Oh, Lord, yeah. Don't Tell Me Nothing About My Man. And I Think I Hate a Man Like You.
And Jelly Roll took that other voice in there.
Yes. Yeah. He knocked on the door and said, Lizzy, come see your man going down the street with Fanny Bryce. Or Fanny something. Jelly was quite a fella.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, he was. Then I Made On The Columbia with Clarence Williams. And I think on a couple of those records, he used... Now, maybe that was King Oliver, that cornet, because I did make a record.
My different kind of man and you're such a cruel papa.
That was with Clarence Williams. That's right. That was with Clarence Williams. That's his number.
Yeah.
That was Clarence Williams' number.
And I believe that had a cornet on it.
Well, that's it. Because I think those were the ones I made with King Oliver. Yeah. Yeah.
And you remember anybody else in the band? Have a clarinet player?
No, I can't remember.
Joe was having a hard time then, huh?

Well, those New York musicians, they was against those Western boys coming in there. That's the guys coming from Chicago, you know? It seemed to give them a hard way to go, you know? And I think that's where his band broke up from him there, you know? I think Russell, this Louis Russell, I think, then took the band over or something. The piano player. Hmm? But then I went, I went, then he started, he was getting jobs like in Atlantic City, you know? I went with him twice to Atlantic City. He's in Ryan. On, yeah, on a couple jobs. We drove there by car, you know?
Did he have any other New Orleans musicians with him? Anybody else remember being outstanding?
From New Orleans? Yeah. I think he did. I think he did. I think Albert Nichols was with him.
Well, that's that Louis Russell bunch, aren't we?

That's King Oliver's bunch, you see? They double-crossed King, and that's where Russell got the bunch. Something came up there, and that's where I think they all swung with Russell. That's the whole bunch that was with King when he came there to New York. Pops Foster? Well, I don't exactly remember, you know, who they were.
I see here in the book you got Lizzie Miles and her Creole jazz hands on Emerson. Four O'clock Blues and Aggravating Papa. You remember anything about that record?

Yeah, but I wouldn't remember who the fellas were. Just like I tell you, you know, they just get any guy, you know, make up a combination like that, you see? So I wouldn't know who they were, who the fellas were. I wouldn't remember them, you know, who they were.
Lizzie Miles and her Melrose Stompers, you remember that bunch?
The Melrose Stompers, what piece was that?

They're for the Vecalion, that's all right, Daddy, and keep on knocking, number two. He's My Man, Mellow Rhythm, that was the instrumental only. Hold Me Parson, He's Red Hot to Me, 20 Grand Blues and Stranger Blues. You don't remember any of those?
No.
Cornette, saxophone, and rhythm.
No, I can't remember. I remember the record, making the record. I made that in, I think, 30, 39. Made that record in 39. Those records in 39.
I just picked up that. That's all right, Daddy, and keep on knocking, number two. I got that myself the other day.
Keep knocking, but you can't come in? Yeah. Yeah, and then Hold Me Parson, I Feel Religion coming on. You got that one?
No, I don't got that. I got to keep on knocking, number two.

And they got one, Hold Me Parson, I Feel Religion coming on, and an awful lot my man ain't got, but what he's got, he's got an awful lot, and what he's got, it sure ain't hard to me. That was a good one.
I see they got composers on this record I got. They got Wiggins, that would be James Wiggins, maybe, huh?
On which record?
On, I believe it's Keep On a Knocking.
Keep Knocking, but you can't come in?
Yeah.
Well, Melrose said that was his, I don't know. Oh, yeah.
What about Big Bill? Did you ever know Big Bill Brooms? Was he on any of his?
No. Miney Jones is the one that got that connection for me with Melrose. Miney Jones, who wrote Caledonia?
Oh, yeah.
Miney Jones. Trouble in Miney. Yeah, yeah, that's right.
Richard M. Jones.
Richard M. Jones, we call him Miney. Yeah, that's right, that's right. Well, that Keep Knocking, that was just the same like the bucket got a hole in it. Yeah, that was the one.
Oh, yeah.
Mm-hmm.
Do you remember I was making any records with Fletcher Anderson?

No, I never made records with Fletcher Anderson. Mm-hmm. The only band that I made records was when I went for the OK, wait for the OK was this white band that was the studio band, then King Oliver and his group. Well, this little, that was a little small combination on the, with that vocabula, keep knocking but you can't come in. That was, I think it was about four, huh? Three or four of them. Yeah, that's all. That's all. Most all of my records was piano. You know, most piano records. Mm-hmm.

Fat Waller, Fat Waller, Willie Smith, the Lion, oh, like I told you, Leroy Smith, I can't think of what his name, Brooks, Brooks, Porter Granger, Jelly Roll Martin, Clarence Johnson, Donald Haywood, Donald Haywood, Russell Robison, Clarence Williams, Clarence Williams, Glover Compton, Hutchinson, but I don't think he's in this country because I think he's a West Indian, he went, when he went abroad, he couldn't come back. numbers but I can remember that one that was the I enjoyed singing and working with them better than anybody that I sing and work with they had an orchestra just weren't when they gave you a 40 introduction and then when you started they got right underneath your voice and everybody was playing you know everybody was playing you know see just sounds like he was floating on the air piano violin two connects trombone I think two saxophone banjo and drums and they were all artists everyone went hit the man I tell you I worked for at the capital he brought them from Atlantic City and the Duke Ellington Fletcher Henderson all those bands that was working around who got the time when they leave their job they came down to sit and listen to them boys play oh they had an orchestra that was really worth sitting down listening to and singing with they were great well I enjoyed I mean I he's he's piano playing you know well and Fat Waller and Willie Smith the line I I enjoyed working with them too but I like

a Dixieland make up a Dixieland band any type of band you like to sing with like right now yes well now at the piano at the piano you want the New Orleans you mean New Orleans a musician anywhere and your favorite from anywhere just my favorite piano player from anywhere well I'd have a fetch while on the piano well not it would be a draw between fat Waller and oil Heinz those is my two favorites I think it would be a draw wish between the two I'd want you know and well now King Oliver was a nice cornet player I liked I like to sing with him and I liked Freddie Kappa too when I worked with both of them I liked both of them you know that's the clan and play Sidney Bechet he tossed my list Sidney Bechet and now wait is the guitar guitarist I can't think of the fellas name that I like I know I made records with him too but I can't think of his name as the guitarist I know I made records with him too but I can't think of his name as the guitarist New York fella Chicago fella no I think he was um I think he was from Long Island young boy a little young boy he was a little young boy he was a little young boy young fella who'd you use on trombone I can't remember I mean who would you like to use on trombone in the band who would you pick out one of the Parrish boys Sidney Parrish's brother I can't remember his name Wilbur Parrish yeah yeah I like him Danny Barker working together now I'm a guitarist I'm a guitarist I can't think of the guy I like him

one of the Parrish boys Sidney Parrish's brother I can't remember his name Wilbur Parrish yeah yeah I like him he and Danny Barker working together now oh yeah yeah well you see I've never heard much of Danny Barker even though Danny Barker roomed with me but I've never heard him out you know playing out I um but I used to be crazy about Lonnie Lonnie Johnson's guitar playing I used to like the way Lonnie played guitar
what about bass players did you pick for that

well uh now bass players uh you see most of the orchestra King Oliver's orchestra was about the only orchestra that I sang with that had a bass player and that was Eddie Garland you see they all uh they didn't have no bass players in those other orchestras oh yeah
drummers you use the drumming

well I never did pay much attention to the drummers on the card they always had to swing low you know see so I never mostly if it was for dancing you'd kind of you know worry about the drumming but I never much my main was uh was uh piano I always liked a good piano player that's the only thing I paid much attention to when did you work with Earl Hines you ever worked with him? no I never worked with Earl Hines but I just like his style of playing I just like the way he plays but I never worked with him
say we uh we've left off something about you coming back from Europe you came back down here yeah well okay
now uh let's say you left Europe and you came back to the capital to New York to New York to the capital
and then you left the capital and went to the Ness club
Ness and then you left the Ness and came back to New York

oh I wait at the BAM I wait the the places I went to New York was at Dash's Inn the capital palace the uh well I double at the capital palace and the cotton club at the same time that was when Jack Johnson first opened the cotton club you know that's who first had the cotton club on Lenox and it was Jack Johnson well I was when I worked there for him I worked at the capital at the same time see but of course it didn't last long because he didn't draw like they thought he was gonna draw you see it looked like he was fronting for the real owners of the place and he didn't draw the crowd that they thought he was gonna draw so then they just closed down and they redecorated and then they uh opened up with the big show with a big show and that's where they sent Piron's band went up there Armand Piron's band because they wanted that Dixieland stuff from down here but instead of them coming up there playing that they came up there playing Paul Whiteman you know all that high class and they didn't want that they wanted that real Dixieland you know see well then after he left Piron left I don't remember who else went in there but I know Piron came from down here to open up at the Viettec Cotton Club you see but they just didn't give them the kind of music that they wanted they wanted that real Dixieland stuff from down here Piron was we had Steve Lewis and Cottrell and all that and you know they was playing all that other kind of stuff that wasn't what they wanted you see and then I worked at the Nes Club I worked at the Bamville I worked at the Strollers Club I worked at the Dash Inn I worked at Herman's Inn I think that's about the only clubs that I worked in About when did you leave New York to come back to New Orleans?

segments.chapter: Childhood and early career in New Orleans
segments.title: Opening of the Mardi Gras Lounge recording, January 1951
segments.summary: Allen announces the date and place, Mardi Gras Lounge on Bourbon Street, with R.W. Greenwood present, and starts with Lizzie's birth.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early career in New Orleans
segments.title: Born on Bourbon Street, 1895; mother's singing; catechism school
segments.summary: Lizzie was born in New Orleans on March 31, 1895. Her mother sang only late in life, and Lizzie began singing in catechism school since there was no money for lessons.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early career in New Orleans
segments.title: Mrs. Atkin's backyard concerts and the first shows
segments.summary: Neighborhood children sang and danced in concerts, the pay rose, and she moved on to the halls and then to touring shows with her sister.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early career in New Orleans
segments.title: Singing at concert-and-ball halls with the early bands
segments.summary: Concerts were followed by dances, with a band hired for each. She sang with musicians such as Kid Ory, King Oliver, Manuel Perez and Bunk Johnson.

segments.chapter: Childhood and early career in New Orleans
segments.title: How she became Lizzie Miles
segments.summary: She explains the billing 'Miles of smiles' and her real name, Elizabeth Landreau and then Pajot. Willie Pajot was her husband's first cousin.

segments.chapter: Names, influences and early blues singers
segments.title: Admired singers: Sophie Tucker and her sister the coon shouter
segments.summary: She went to hear Sophie Tucker at the Palace Theater and admired her sister's shouting and eye-rolling style.

segments.chapter: Names, influences and early blues singers
segments.title: Other musical relatives
segments.summary: No other sisters sang. She knows of no musicians on her father's side, because she did not know that part of the family.

segments.chapter: Names, influences and early blues singers
segments.title: Ma Rainey, Mamie Smith and New Orleans blues singers
segments.summary: She worked on the same dates as Ma Rainey and heard the Smiths. She calls Mamie Smith's Crazy Blues the first popular blues record, and mentions Tilly Johnson and Ann Cook.

segments.chapter: Bucktown, Chicago and the cabaret years
segments.title: First cabaret job at Bucktown with Manuel Mineta's band
segments.summary: Her first nightclub job was in Bucktown, singing Dardanella with Manuel Mineta's band. They try to recall the other players, including Amos White on cornet and Zip on clarinet.

segments.chapter: Bucktown, Chicago and the cabaret years
segments.title: From Bucktown to Chicago: King Oliver at the Dreamland and other cabarets
segments.summary: She came to like cabaret work and went to Chicago, where she joined King Oliver's band at the Dreamland. She then worked briefly at Freddie Keppard's place and with Glover Compton at the De Luxe.

segments.chapter: Bucktown, Chicago and the cabaret years
segments.title: Glover Compton and returning to New Orleans
segments.summary: Talk of Glover Compton and his wife Nettie Lewis, with whom she worked. She then went home to New Orleans after the war.

segments.title: Circus during the war and the flu epidemic
segments.summary: She toured with a circus during the First World War and caught the flu and pneumonia. She was told to stop singing for a year, and later went to Bucktown for fresh air.

segments.title: Return to Chicago and Spencer Williams proposes a New York trip
segments.summary: After a Springfield cabaret job she met Spencer Williams in Chicago, who took her to New York for record auditions. Edith Wilson got the Blackbirds job instead.

segments.title: New York auditions, Harlem clubs and the Paris engagement as La Rose Noire
segments.summary: She worked at Dash's Inn and the Capitol on Lenox Avenue, then went to Paris with Danny Wilson and Ali Laguerre. There she worked at Chez Michels and became La Rose Noire.

segments.title: Her first records: OKeh, Brunswick and the Spencer Williams songs
segments.summary: Allen asks who accompanied her records. She recalls an OKeh studio band, pianist Clarence Johnson, and Russell Robinson on the Brunswick sides.

segments.title: Records for Victor and with Jelly Roll Morton
segments.summary: She recalls Man of War Blues and the sessions with Jelly Roll Morton, who knocked at the door during a take.

segments.title: Records with Clarence Williams and King Oliver; the Oliver band in New York
segments.summary: She made records for Columbia with Clarence Williams, probably with King Oliver on cornet. She describes Oliver's band struggling in New York and Louis Russell taking it over.

segments.title: Later labels: Emerson, Melrose Stompers, Vocalion and Richard M. Jones
segments.summary: Allen runs through discography items. She recalls the 1939 Vocalion sides, Richard M. Jones as the connection to Melrose, and that she never recorded with Fletcher Henderson's band.

segments.title: Piano players she worked with and Charlie Taylor's orchestra
segments.summary: She lists the many pianists she worked with, names Fats Waller and Willie Smith as favorites, and praises Charlie Taylor's orchestra, which she most enjoyed singing with.

segments.title: Dream band: pianists, Oliver, Bechet, guitar, trombone, bass and drums
segments.summary: She picks her ideal band, with Fats Waller or Earl Hines on piano, King Oliver or Freddie Keppard on cornet, Sidney Bechet, Lonnie Johnson on guitar, and Eddie Garland on bass.

segments.chapter: New York clubs and return home
segments.title: The Capitol Palace, the Cotton Club and Piron's band in New York
segments.summary: Back from Europe she worked at the Capitol and Cotton Club. Piron's New Orleans band disappointed the Cotton Club audience, and she lists the other clubs she worked.

segments.title: Barmaid work in New Orleans after her return
segments.summary: Back in New Orleans around 1938 she tended bar on Rampart Street and sang along to the music box. She stayed because of her mother's illness.

segments.title: Opening at the Paddock in September and meeting Sid Davilla
segments.summary: She sang at the Paddock for eight weeks, and asked Sid Davilla for an audition at the Mardi Gras Lounge.

segments.title: Papa Stopper's radio program and the route to the Mardi Gras Lounge
segments.summary: Her letter led to an appearance on the radio program and a call from Joe Mares. She auditioned for Mr. Valenti at the Parisian Room, then was sent to Davilla.

segments.title: Her old stage costumes
segments.summary: She still wears dresses she bought for her mother in 1923 and shoes from Paris, kept in a trunk with mothballs.

segments.title: Movies: the circus picture and Tip Tap Toe
segments.summary: She appeared in a circus film starring Bessie Love and in Tip Tap Toe, singing Three's a Crowd. She did no more because of a contract dispute.

segments.title: Clarence Williams and the Chicago picnic; calling each other 'cuz'
segments.summary: Clarence Williams was connected to Columbia and OKeh. She tells how he got stage fright at a big Chicago event and played in the wrong key. The musicians all called each other 'cuz'.

segments.title: High spots and best job
segments.summary: She enjoyed big audiences and says she made the most money at the Nest Club.

segments.title: Bands at the Nest Club
segments.summary: Sam Wooding's orchestra and Danny Wilson's band played at the Nest, and Wooding then left for the Club Alabama and Europe.

segments.title: Knowing Duke Ellington's musicians; Bonnie's family
segments.summary: She knew many Ellington men from the Capitol, including Sonny Greer, Braud, Barney Bigard and Benny Carter. She talks about Bigard's father, family and relatives.
